title: Asa Relies on Aram and Ends Badly
summary: When Baasha of Israel fortifies Ramah to blockade Judah, Asa sends the temple and palace treasures to Ben-hadad of Aram to buy an alliance, and the plan works. But the seer Hanani rebukes Asa for relying on a foreign king instead of the LORD, and Asa jails him and oppresses some of the people. In his last years Asa suffers a severe disease in his feet and seeks only physicians, not the LORD, and he is buried with great honor.
story: The first half of Asa's story (chapters 14 and 15) showed a king who sought God, relied on him against Zerah, and led his people into covenant. This chapter is the sad second half. The same verb that described his faith in 14:11, rely, now describes his trust in a foreign king. The Chronicler presents Asa as a warning that a good beginning does not guarantee a faithful ending. His son Jehoshaphat, whose reign fills chapters 17 to 20, will face similar tests with alliances and will receive similar prophetic warnings.
historical:
The parallel account in 1 Kings 15:16-22 records the conflict with Baasha and the alliance with Ben-hadad, and 1 Kings 15:23 mentions Asa's diseased feet in old age. Chronicles adds Hanani's rebuke, Asa's harsh response, and the detail that he did not seek the LORD in his illness. Baasha ruled the northern kingdom about 909 to 886 BC. Ramah lay only a few miles north of Jerusalem on the main north-south road, so fortifying it would have choked Judah's access to the north. Ben-hadad, king of Aram (the Aramean kingdom centered at Damascus, in modern Syria), responded to Asa's payment by attacking Israel's northern towns: Ijon, Dan, and Abel-maim (called Abel-beth-maacah in Kings) lay near the sources of the Jordan. Asa then used Baasha's building materials to fortify Geba and Mizpah on his own northern frontier.

The dates in verses 1 and 12 raise a chronological puzzle. According to 1 Kings 16:8, Baasha died and was succeeded in Asa's twenty-sixth year, so he could not have campaigned in Asa's thirty-sixth. Some scholars propose that the thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth years (15:19, 16:1) are counted from the division of the kingdom rather than from Asa's accession, which would place the war around Asa's sixteenth year. Others suggest a copying error in the numbers, or that the Chronicler has arranged the dates to structure Asa's reign theologically into a long faithful period followed by decline. The difficulty is real and the solutions remain debated.
cultural:
A treaty in the ancient Near East was a formal agreement between kings, often sealed with gifts or tribute. Asa's message speaks of a treaty that had existed between their fathers and asks Ben-hadad to break his current treaty with Baasha. Buying a larger power's help against a neighbor was a common strategy, but in Israel's prophetic tradition it was repeatedly condemned as trusting in human power rather than in God (Isaiah 31:1 makes a similar charge about Egypt).

Seeking physicians was not itself wrong. The Old Testament describes healing remedies, and the Chronicler's complaint is that Asa sought only physicians and not the LORD. Some interpreters suggest the physicians may have been associated with foreign healing practices or magic, but the text does not say so. The great fire at Asa's burial was not cremation, which Israel did not practice for its honored dead. It was a ceremonial burning of spices in the king's honor, also mentioned in Jeremiah 34:5 and withheld from the disgraced king Jehoram in 21:19.
literary: The chapter is built as a deliberate contrast with chapter 14. There, Asa relied on the LORD against a vast army and won; here he relies on the king of Aram and gains a short-term success that the prophet calls folly. Hanani's speech makes the contrast explicit by reminding Asa of the Cushites and Libyans. The verb rely appears three times in verses 7 and 8, and the verb seek in verse 12 closes the story by showing that Asa, whose reign began with a command to seek the LORD (14:4), ends it by seeking only human help. Verse 9 states the principle behind the whole book of Chronicles in a single sentence: the LORD looks for those whose hearts are fully devoted to him in order to strengthen them.

outline.t: Baasha fortifies Ramah, and Asa buys Ben-hadad's help
Hanani's rebuke and Asa's angry response

doctrines.note: Asa's failure is not unbelief in God's existence but misplaced reliance. Hanani's rebuke shows that faith is a matter of where one leans one's weight in a crisis, and that past trust does not substitute for present trust.
Verse 9 pictures God's eyes ranging over the whole earth, looking for those whose hearts are wholly his so that he may show himself strong for them. God's care is active and searching, not passive.
Asa's anger at the prophet, his imprisonment of Hanani, and his oppression of the people show how one compromise can harden into resistance against correction.

words.note: Sha'an, to lean or rely. It appears three times in Hanani's rebuke and recalls 13:18 and 14:11. The Chronicler uses the word as the test of a king: on whom does he put his weight when the pressure comes?

Shut, to rove or range to and fro. It describes the eyes of the LORD moving across the whole earth. The picture is not of surveillance for punishment but of God seeking out the loyal to strengthen them.

Sakal, to act foolishly. In the Old Testament folly is not low intelligence but a moral and spiritual failure to live in light of God. Asa's strategy was politically clever and still foolish in this sense.
Rapha, to heal; the participle means healers or physicians. The same verb describes God as Israel's healer (Exodus 15:26). The irony of verse 12 is that Asa sought the healers but not the Healer.

christ: Hanani's word that the eyes of the LORD range over the earth to strengthen those whose hearts are wholly his describes a God who seeks people out. Jesus described his own mission in those terms: he came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). Asa's failure to seek God in his illness also stands in contrast to the crowds in the gospels who brought their sick to Jesus, and to the New Testament's instruction to bring illness to God in prayer while also caring for the body (James 5:14-15). The Bible's story needed a king whose heart remained fully devoted to God to the end, and the New Testament presents Jesus as that king, who trusted his Father even on the cross (Luke 23:46). The link is thematic, not a prediction in the text.

hard.q: Is it wrong for a believer to go to a doctor?
hard.a: The chapter does not condemn medicine. Its complaint is that Asa sought only the physicians and did not seek the LORD, which fits the pattern of the whole chapter: he relied on human resources in place of God. Elsewhere Scripture treats healing remedies with approval, as when Isaiah prescribes a poultice of figs for Hezekiah's illness (2 Kings 20:7), and the New Testament includes Luke, whom Paul calls the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14). Some interpreters think Asa's physicians may have used magical or foreign religious practices, but the text doesn't say so, and it's better not to build on that guess. Christian teaching has generally held that seeking medical care and seeking God belong together, and that the danger lies in trusting any human help as though God were not needed.

questions: Asa trusted God against a huge army but not against a smaller threat years later. Why might long experience sometimes make trust harder rather than easier?
Asa jailed the prophet who told him the truth. How do you respond when someone points out that you have relied on the wrong thing?
Hanani said the LORD looks for those whose hearts are fully devoted to him. What does a fully devoted heart look like on an ordinary day?
